title: Offshore Industry Sends Urgent Call To EU Policymakers For Fit-For-Purpose EU ETS And MRV Framework
summary: Offshore industry associations are petitioning the EU to delay their inclusion in the EU ETS from 2027, citing an "unfit" MRV framework that could "distort competition." This "urgent call" suspiciously aligns with an effort to circumvent upcoming carbon costs, despite their self-proclaimed role in Europe's energy transition. Robust, unambiguous emissions accounting is critical for all vessels; special exemptions or delays only enable continued high-carbon operations under the guise of "strategic assets."
content:
Eight maritime associations including the Royal Belgian Shipowners’ Association (KBRV) send an open letter to EU policymakers urging them to ensure a fit-for-purpose framework for the European offshore sector under the current EU ETS review.

The offshore shipping sector is a strategic asset to the European economy, playing a leading role in the continent’s energy transition, energy security and industrial competitiveness.

Yet the current EU ETS framework, entering into force beginning 2027 for offshore vessels, will distort competition and create opportunities for circumvention, based on a Monitoring, Reporting, and Verification (MRV) framework that was not designed for offshore operations and is widely recognised as not fit for purpose.

The sector strongly urges EU policymakers to first ensure that a fit-for purpose activity-based MRV framework is operational, before the inclusion of offshore vessels above 5000GT in EU ETS from next year onwards.

Below is the open letter the sector has addressed to the European Parliament and members of the Council

EU ETS REVIEW: GET THE FRAMEWORK RIGHT FOR EUROPE’S OFFSHORE SECTOR

Open letter to Members of the European Parliament and EU Member States’ Permanent Representatives.

Europe’s offshore industry is a strategic asset. European companies are global leaders in the construction and maintenance of offshore windfarms, seabed, subsea infrastructure and other critical maritime infrastructure. Their vessels play an essential role in Europe’s energy transition, energy security and industrial competitiveness.

The undersigned associations fully support the EU’s climate objectives and the principle of carbon pricing. However, the planned inclusion of offshore vessels above 5000GT in the EU ETS from 2027 will impose significant financial obligations, distort competition and create opportunities for circumvention, based on an MRV reporting framework that was not designed for offshore operations and is widely recognised as not fit for purpose.

Our three calls to EU policymakers

1. Safeguard the international level playing field for offshore vessels. Identical offshore operations must face the same CO₂ costs, regardless of the port from which a vessel operates. The revised legislation should establish a clear activity-based system and close loopholes that will incentivise operators to mobilise vessels from non-EU ports.

2. Get the framework right. Define offshore activities, worksites and ports of call clearly, including seabed-related work. Replace unsuitable cargo, passenger and transport-work metrics and unnecessary voyage-by-voyage reporting with proportionate, harmonised, aggregated reporting.

3. Get the timing right. Do not impose ETS surrender obligations on offshore vessels until a revised, fit-for purpose MRV framework is implemented and demonstrated its ability to support reliable, fair and consistent emissions accounting. This is a sequencing request, not an exemption from carbon pricing!

Why this matters

Unlike conventional shipping, offshore vessels do not primarily transport cargo or passengers between ports. They perform specialised, project-based activities such as installation, construction, maintenance, dredging and inspection at offshore worksites. Applying traditional concepts such as cargo, transport work and voyage based reporting therefore does not reflect their operational reality.

More importantly, the current framework will distort the level playing field. Equivalent offshore activities can face different ETS exposure depending on the vessel’s deployment port: emissions will be fully covered when operating from an EU port, while the same activities from a non-EU port fall outside the EU ETS. This will shift offshore activity outside Europe, result in carbon leakage and weaken Europe’s strategic offshore capacity.

Offshore vessels of above 5000GT are nevertheless due to enter the EU ETS from 2027, before a fit-for purpose activity-based MRV framework is operational. Given the major flaws in the current methodology, this approach is disproportionate. The EU ETS and MRV review should therefore ensure that the reporting framework is fixed before ETS surrender obligations apply.

We urge the European Parliament and the Council to use the review to deliver one clear, fair and enforceable regime for offshore vessels.
